facts.claim: "Because" was released on June 8, 2022 as the second single from Danger Mouse and Black Thought's collaborative album Cheat Codes, featuring Joey Bada$$, Russ and Dylan Cartlidge.
It follows "No Gold Teeth," the first single from Cheat Codes, and The Fader calls it a posse cut.
Cheat Codes is produced by Danger Mouse. The album credits list Black Thought on vocals and engineering, and Danger Mouse on production and engineering.

Writing credits for "Because" list Dorian Burton (Danger Mouse's legal name), Dylan Cartlidge, Herman Kelly, Jo-Vaughn Virginie Scott (Joey Bada$$), Russell James Vitale (Russ) and Trotter (Black Thought). The track runs 4:41.
Danger Mouse said the two of them were the only people in the room when they recorded the album. He also said they ended up keeping everything instead of just demoing it.
Joey Bada$$ said he was a big fan of both Black Thought and Danger Mouse. He called Black Thought one of the greatest rappers ever, and said joining the record was a no-brainer when they asked.
Russ said that collaborating with one of the greatest lyricists of all time, alongside Danger Mouse, was an honor.
Black Thought's verse reflects on violence and his upbringing. It ends with the line about dying "just because."
Consequence describes the track as luxurious, retro-soul Danger Mouse production, with a hook from Dylan Cartlidge that sounds time-warped.

Cheat Codes was first mooted around 2006 under the name Dangerous Thoughts. Scheduling conflicts held it up until the pair reconvened in 2018. It marks Danger Mouse's first hip-hop album since his 2005 DANGERDOOM album with MF DOOM, The Mouse and the Mask. Black Thought had made three solo albums since The Roots' last record.

research.lineage: The song is a posse cut in the boom-bap and sample-based soul-rap tradition. It pairs The Roots' Black Thought with Gnarls Barkley and DANGERDOOM producer Danger Mouse, with younger guest rappers Joey Bada$$ and Russ and UK vocalist Dylan Cartlidge.

draft:
The hook keeps saying **"Because"** as if a reason is coming, and none ever arrives. Dylan Cartlidge sings it as a weary half-answer, a voice Consequence heard as time-warped: "Because this love is so non-desirable." Then Black Thought takes that empty word and closes his verse with it: "Don't need a reason to die, we die just because." The chorus sounds like a love song gone sour. The verse shows it was about something much heavier.

That turn is the emotional key. Black Thought's verse, which Paste reads as a reflection on violence and upbringing, moves through cheap candy from the deli, street games, a cellmate reading Machiavelli, and a narrator turning from one faith to the next looking for something that holds. The images come fast and dense, the way the best of his writing does, but the feeling under them is a tired shrug at how cheap life gets treated. He doesn't rage. He reports, and that restraint is what hurts. The verse before it pushes the same weight further back, through Elmina's door of no return and a narrator screaming into the ocean for comfort, history and grief stacked on top of each other with nowhere to put them down.

Danger Mouse keeps the bed calm underneath all of it. A steady hip-hop beat with a firm snare, a simple bass line circling, warm sustained keys, and a clean arpeggiated guitar figure. The groove is laid-back, the mix clean and dry, and the sung hook stands alone without harmonies stacked behind it. Consequence called it luxurious retro soul, and that fits the tradition the song sits in, sample-minded soul-rap with boom-bap bones. The comfort of the sound is the point. It lets hard verses go down easy, then stick.

The Fader called it a posse cut, and the guests widen the frame. One verse sets skateboard nostalgia beside the memory of people shot outside a dry cleaner, Cohibas in Costa Rica beside stop-and-frisk, a parent's warning so the streets "would never father" him. Success hasn't erased anything, and the verse ends by admitting you don't know that part of him. The last verse is the most exposed: a toxic marriage handed down, money that broke a family, chasing approval while knowing better, and "I don't vacation, dawg, I guilt trip." It's self-justification and self-disgust in the same breath, and the verse doesn't settle between them.

Danger Mouse and Black Thought first floated this partnership around 2006 and only reconvened in 2018. You can hear the patience in it.

It sticks because the hook keeps promising a reason, and by the end you understand the missing reason is the wound.
